name: Noni fruit extract
lead: Noni fruit extract comes from Morinda citrifolia, a tropical shrub of the coffee family (Rubiaceae) that Polynesian sailors carried across the Pacific. The pungent fruit was eaten as a famine food, and its leaves, bark and roots were used in traditional medicine and as dyes.[1] Today it is sold as juice, powders, capsules and as an ingredient in lotions, soaps and seed oils.[1]

In appearance care, noni is positioned as an antioxidant botanical for skin and hair. Its pitch rests on constituents such as anthraquinones, iridoids, flavonoids and scopoletin.[1] Laboratory work has reported that an anthraquinone from the fruit induced extracellular matrix synthesis in cultured human skin fibroblasts, the kind of activity associated with firmer-looking skin,[3] and a formulation study paired noni with pandan leaf extract in an anti-dandruff shampoo.[4]

Wikipedia states there is no confirmed evidence of clinical efficacy for any intended use, and it cites a 2024 review linking noni supplements and drinks to a risk of liver disease through anthraquinone exposure.[1] In July 2018 the US FDA issued a warning letter to a noni marketer over unapproved drug claims.[1] No trial of noni on skin appearance was identified.

paras: Morinda citrifolia is a shrub or small tree reaching about 6 m, with large opposite leaves, white tubular flowers and a multiple fruit that gives off a strong odour when ripe. It flowers and fruits year-round, tolerates saline soils and drought, and was assessed as Least Concern by the IUCN in 2024.[1]

Austronesian voyagers took the plant into the Pacific as a canoe plant, and it is now cultivated across the tropics and widely naturalised.[1] Indigenous communities ate the fruit during famines, which earned it the nickname starvation fruit, and on some islands it was a staple eaten raw or cooked. Southeast Asian and Aboriginal Australian cooks used it with salt or in curries, and leaves appear in Thai and Cambodian dishes.[1] Polynesians reportedly used green fruit, leaves and roots as a general tonic, and bark and roots served as dyes, including by Yolngu artists in Arnhem Land who dye pandanus fibres with it.[1]

Reported constituents include anthraquinones (among them damnacanthal), lignans, polysaccharides, flavonoids, iridoids, scopoletin, catechin, beta-sitosterol, fatty acids and alkaloids. Fruit powder supplies moderate carbohydrate and fibre, while the juice is sparse in nutrients.[1]

A pharmacokinetic study used scopoletin as a marker of noni exposure and noted the lack of product standardisation across the many noni products sold worldwide.[2] Food-technology work has examined stabilising noni extract by microencapsulation with gum arabic and maltodextrin for powders.[9]

sections.h: Use in skin and hair care
paras: Consumer noni products include lotions, soaps and seed oil.[1] Cosmetic positioning generally leans on antioxidant and skin-conditioning claims. A 2005 laboratory study reported that an anthraquinone isolated from noni fruit induced extracellular matrix synthesis in normal human fibroblasts,[3] and a 2021 formulation study combined noni and pandan leaf extracts as a candidate anti-dandruff shampoo.[4]

In bodybuilding forums, noni appeared mainly as an oral supplement. A 2001 T Nation thread asked about Morinda citrifolia and the alkaloid xeronin in the context of recovery, and a 2006 thread discussed noni juice opinions, with posters pointing to Wikipedia's description of promotion of the juice as a cure for various conditions.[10][11] These are individual forum posts rather than a body of practice.

Preclinical and food-science studies have examined noni extract for other purposes: laxative activity and low organ toxicity in mice,[20] glucose and lipid metabolism in diabetic mice,[21] memory impairment in mice,[12] antibacterial activity against Listeria as a produce wash,[13] and effects in livestock and shrimp feed.[14][15] A periodontal study evaluated noni extract as a bone regenerative material for intrabony defects using clinical and cone-beam CT assessment.[16] These studies address health or agricultural endpoints rather than skin appearance.
Wikipedia notes that anthraquinones can be harmful and cites a 2024 review in Medicine (Baltimore) reporting a risk of liver disease from noni supplements, beverages, powders, oils and leaves.[1]

On 18 July 2018 the FDA issued a warning letter to Hawaiian Organic Noni, LLC for marketing unapproved drugs and making health claims under the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act.[1] Published pharmacokinetic work has stated that noni products lack standardisation and that no optimal dose or dosing interval has been established.[2]

No trials of noni on skin or appearance were found. A phase I study of noni in 51 advanced cancer patients sought a maximum tolerated dose using quality-of-life measures; the maximum tolerated dose was reported as 12 g daily in capsules, with no dose-limiting toxicity found and withdrawals at the next level attributed to the difficulty of swallowing so many capsules.[5] A phase I pharmacokinetic study gave freeze-dried fruit capsules to nine healthy volunteers and found that scopoletin entered plasma rapidly, with low bioavailability and considerable variation between people.[2]

A randomized, double-blind, crossover, placebo-controlled study in 30 healthy subjects found that 1 g of noni extract altered alcohol absorption timing and lowered blood acetaldehyde compared with placebo.[6] A registered study of an iridoid-enriched beverage examined skin autofluorescence as a marker of oxidative stress (NCT01597076, n=34),[7] and a phase II prostate cancer trial was terminated after six participants.[8] A phase I study in cancer patients began in 2001 (NCT00033878).[17]

card.summary: A Pacific fruit extract sold as an antioxidant; skin evidence is lab-only and liver-safety concerns are documented for oral products.
card.note: A 2024 review links oral noni products to liver disease risk; FDA 2018 warning letter on claims.

quick.overview:
Noni is a tropical fruit used traditionally in the Pacific and now sold as juice, supplements and in cosmetics as an antioxidant botanical.

Wikipedia reports no confirmed clinical efficacy for any use. Skin research is limited to cell studies.
quick.mechanism: An anthraquinone from the fruit was reported to boost extracellular matrix synthesis in cultured fibroblasts; this has not been tested in people.
quick.risks: Anthraquinones can be harmful, and a 2024 review is cited as linking oral noni products to liver disease. The FDA issued a 2018 warning letter over drug claims.
